content: Pneumonia is a serious lung infection that remains the leading cause of death in children under the age of five worldwide. Chest physiotherapy is often used as an additional treatment for pneumonia, with the aim of clearing inflammatory exudates, tracheobronchial secretions, and airway obstructions, thereby reducing airway resistance, improving breathing, and enhancing gas exchange. This review updates a previous analysis published in 2013 and evaluates the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy in children with pneumonia. The objective of this review was to determine whether chest physiotherapy could reduce the time to clinical resolution in children aged from birth to 18 years, regardless of gender or type of pneumonia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, LILACS, Web of Science, and PEDro, as well as clinical trial registries such as ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing chest physiotherapy to no physiotherapy in children with pneumonia were included. The review incorporated six RCTs involving 559 children aged 29 days to 12 years, all of whom were treated as inpatients. Pneumonia severity was classified as moderate in one trial, severe in two trials, and unspecified in three trials. The studies evaluated five different chest physiotherapy interventions: conventional chest physiotherapy (three studies, 211 children), positive expiratory pressure (one study, 72 children), continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) (one study, 94 children), bubble CPAP (bCPAP) (one study, 225 children), and assisted autogenic drainage (one study, 29 children). These trials were conducted in Bangladesh, Brazil, China, Egypt, and South Africa. Overall, the studies were considered to have a low risk of bias, although blinding of participants was not feasible in most cases. However, the lack of blinding was deemed unlikely to influence the outcomes. One study on bCPAP reported three deaths in the physiotherapy group (79 children) compared to 20 deaths in the control group (146 children), with a risk ratio (RR) of 0.28 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.08 to 0.90; 225 children; low-quality evidence). No deaths were reported in one study on assisted autogenic drainage (29 children) and one study on conventional chest physiotherapy (72 children). It remains uncertain whether chest physiotherapy techniques, including bCPAP, assisted autogenic drainage, and conventional chest physiotherapy, reduced the duration of hospital stays (mean difference [MD] 0.10 days, 95% CI -0.56 to 0.76; four studies; low-quality evidence). The clinical parameters used to define clinical resolution varied across studies. Two small studies found no significant difference in fever resolution between children receiving physiotherapy (conventional chest physiotherapy or assisted autogenic drainage) and those in the control group. Of the five studies that assessed peripheral oxygen saturation levels, only two reported greater improvement with chest physiotherapy (CPAP and conventional chest physiotherapy). However, it was unclear whether respiratory rate improved following conventional chest physiotherapy (MD -2.25 breaths/min, 95% CI -5.17 to 0.68; two studies, 122 children; low-quality evidence). Adverse events were assessed in two studies, but only one reported any events, with a risk ratio of 1.28 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.67; two studies, 254 children; low-quality evidence). In conclusion, the evidence from this review does not allow for reliable conclusions regarding the effectiveness of chest physiotherapy in children with pneumonia. The small number of included trials, variability in study characteristics, and inconsistent statistical reporting limit the findings. Future research should focus on adequately powered studies with standardized chest physiotherapy techniques, clearly defined outcomes (such as duration of leukocytosis and airway clearance), and thorough reporting of adverse effects.
